extracted.intended_audience: musicians, music producers, DJs, and general readers interested in the practice and legalities of music sampling
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of musical sampling covering its definition, technical methods, cultural impact, sample sources/libraries, and the legal and ethical requirements around clearance and copyright. Useful for producers, DJs, and anyone seeking to understand how sampling is done and regulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Sampling is the reuse of a portion (or sample) of a sound recording in another recording; samples may comprise elements such as rhythm, melody, speech, or sound effects and might be only a fragment or a longer portion of music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Samples are often layered, equalized, sped up or slowed down, repitched, looped, or otherwise manipulated and are usually integrated using samplers or software such as digital audio workstations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical manipulation practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers commonly manipulate samples by layering, equalizing, changing tempo (sped up or slowed down), repitching, looping, or otherwise altering the audio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These manipulations are standard production techniques used to integrate samples musically; modern DAWs and samplers increase possibilities for manipulation and integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of samplers and DAWs
rubrics_metrics.description: Samples are recorded, edited, and integrated using electronic instruments (samplers) or software such as digital audio workstations (DAWs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically hardware samplers (Fairlight CMI, Akai MPC, E-mu) enabled sampling; today most sampling work happens in DAWs like Pro Tools and Ableton Live. Samplers allow assignment of samples to pads/keys for performance and sequencing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common sample sources and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Commonly sampled elements include strings, basslines, drum loops, vocal hooks or entire bars of music, especially from soul records; specific widely sampled breaks (e.g., the Amen break, 'Funky Drummer', 'Think' break) are frequent building blocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers historically mined funk, soul and obscure records for drum breaks and hooks; sample selection often reflects genre practice (e.g., hip-hop's use of drum breaks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample libraries and sample packs as legal/creative sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Samples are distributed in sample libraries (sample packs) produced commercially or by producers; these are a common source for contemporary music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using pre-cleared or commercial sample libraries (e.g., Zero-G, Spectrasonics, Jam Pack, Splice, Kingsway Music Library) can simplify clearance and reduce legal risk; public/open collections (e.g., Library of Congress open-source samples) offer copyright-free material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpolation as an alternative to sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpolation is recreating a recording instead of sampling the original sound recording; it requires only the permission of the owners of the musical content (composition/lyrics), not the owners of the recording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpolation gives more freedom to alter constituent components (separate guitar and drum tracks) and avoids needing a license to the original sound recording, though composition/rightsholder permission is still required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearance requirement to legally use a sample
rubrics_metrics.description: To legally use a sample, an artist must acquire legal permission from the copyright holder; sampling without permission can breach the copyright of the original sound recording, of the composition and lyrics, and of the performances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clearance (acquiring permission) can be lengthy and complex and may be prohibitively expensive; moral rights/crediting concerns may also apply. Labels and licensing companies sometimes 'pre-clear' material to simplify the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple rights may need clearance
rubrics_metrics.description: Sampling can implicate multiple separate rights: the sound recording copyright, the composition/lyrics copyright, and performers' rights (performances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers must identify and clear each relevant rightsholder; failure to do so risks infringement and lawsuits. In practice tracing owners can be difficult due to corporate mergers and lost records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-law variability on de minimis and licensing
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have taken different positions on whether unlicensed sampling is permitted: some rulings found that even minimal unlicensed sampling could be infringement, while others allowed de minimis use or permitted modified/unrecognizable samples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notable cases: Grand Upright Music, Ltd. v. Warner Bros. (1991) and Bridgeport Music v. Dimension Films (2005) held unlicensed sampling can infringe (Bridgeport: 'Get a license or do not sample'). VMG Salsoul v. Ciccone (2016, Ninth Circuit) and a 2019 European Court of Justice ruling (recognizable vs. unrecognizable modified samples) show alternate outcomes; jurisdiction matters and precedents differ by circuit/country.

rubrics_metrics.name: De minimis threshold is unsettled and jurisdiction-specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a very short or altered sample requires a license depends on jurisdiction and specific case law; some courts hold all samples require a license regardless of length, others apply de minimis principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a six-second, three-note sample was found de minimis in one case (James Newton v. Beastie Boys), while Bridgeport's Sixth Circuit decision required licenses for all samples. Producers should assume risk varies by jurisdiction and case history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical and economic barriers for clearing samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearance can be financially and administratively prohibitive for less successful artists; the process is easier for successful acts with label support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bedroom producers may find clearing samples nearly impossible; historically some albums (e.g., Paul's Boutique) cleared many samples affordably in a different legal climate, but modern clearance costs can restrict sample-based work to better-resourced artists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical and moral considerations (credit and compensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sampling raises moral-rights and ethical questions: original artists may not be credited or receive royalties, and performers/creators can feel exploited or see sampling as theft rather than homage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as the Amen break and 'Funky Drummer' performers illustrate unpaid or uncredited widespread reuse; some commentators argue for compensation systems or musicological bases for apportioning how much composition a sample comprises when negotiating splits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry practices and informal rules influencing sample selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical informal practices governed sampling (e.g., 'unspoken' rules forbidding sampling recent records, reissues, other hip-hop records or non-vinyl sources); these evolved as sampling became widespread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Producers may still avoid obvious or recent sources to reduce legal risk; using obscure recordings has been a common tactic to lower detection/clearance cost, though it does not remove legal liability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling as cultural practice and creative evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Sampling is both a foundation of genres (notably hip-hop) and a debated creative act: some view it as creative recontextualization, others as plagiarism or theft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a work that uses samples consider cultural context, creativity of manipulation/recontextualization, and whether the sampling introduces new expression (arguments invoked in fair use analyses and artistic criticism).
